title: AutoKaggle: A Multi-Agent Framework for Autonomous Data Science Competitions

contributions.purpose: Provide end-to-end autonomous handling of complex tabular data-science pipelines (Kaggle competitions), going beyond prior one-step or knowledge-base-dependent approaches while keeping users in the loop.
contributions.mechanism: AutoKaggle, a multi-agent framework with a phase-based workflow (six phases: background understanding, preliminary EDA, data cleaning, in-depth EDA, feature engineering, model building/validation/prediction) executed by five specialized agents (Reader, Planner, Developer, Reviewer, Summarizer) with customizable human intervention points.
contributions.evaluation: On 8 selected Kaggle competitions, AutoKaggle achieves 0.85 valid submission rate and 0.82 comprehensive score; reported as competitive performance above average human level; GPT-4o variant highest comprehensive score in 5 of 8 tasks (Table 1).
contributions.domain: LLM multi-agent systems / automated data science
contributions.source_quote: We propose AutoKaggle, a novel multi-agent framework for Kaggle data science competi-tions, achieving high task completion rates and competitive performance above the average human level in our evaluations.

contributions.purpose: Ensure robust and correct code generation despite the logical complexity of data-science tasks.
contributions.mechanism: Phase-based workflow with multi-agent collaboration incorporating an iterative development loop of code execution, code debugging (using error messages plus history), and predefined per-phase unit testing to verify syntactic correctness and logical consistency.
contributions.evaluation: Ablation on debugging times shows comprehensive score varies with debugging iterations (Figure 5); the unit-testing/debugging loop underpins the 0.85 valid submission rate across 8 tasks.
contributions.domain: LLM multi-agent systems / automated data science
contributions.source_quote: We introduce a phase-based workflow integrated with multi-agent collaboration, incorpo-rating iterative debugging and unit testing, which systematically addresses the complexities of data science tasks and ensures robust, correct code generation.

contributions.purpose: Improve code-generation efficiency/quality and reduce reliance on LLM domain knowledge for common data-science operations.
contributions.mechanism: A machine learning tools library of validated, expert-written functions and custom tools for data cleaning, feature engineering, and model building/validation/prediction, combined with self-generated code.
contributions.evaluation: Tool ablation (No Tools vs DC Tools vs DC & FE Tools vs All Tools) shows completion rate and comprehensive score improve as more validated tools are added (Figure showing CR/CS per task).
contributions.domain: LLM multi-agent systems / automated data science
contributions.source_quote: We develop a machine learning tools library and integrate it into our framework, enhancing code generation efficiency and quality for complex data science tasks.

contributions.purpose: Address the transparency/interpretability gap in existing data-science automation and make the system educational.
contributions.mechanism: Comprehensive reporting system that generates detailed reports after each phase and at competition end, documenting the decision-making process, key findings, actions, and reasoning.
contributions.evaluation: Qualitative: reports make workflows transparent and increase user trust; positioned as both a solution provider and an educational tool (no separate quantitative metric).
contributions.domain: LLM multi-agent systems / automated data science
contributions.source_quote: We implement a comprehensive reporting system that provides detailed insights into the decision-making process at each phase, making AutoKaggle both a solution provider and an educational tool for data science competitions, thereby contributing to the democratization of data science skills.

self_declared_provenance.quote: Previous studies have similarly focused on addressing problems in the data science domain, but many of these approaches suffer from limited scalability due to heavy reliance on pre-constructed expert knowledge bases (Guo et al., 2024) or the need for historical data as experience pools (Zhang et al., 2024a). Recently, the AIDE (Schmidt et al., 2024) framework demonstrated strong perfor-mance in Mle-Bench (Chan et al., 2024). However, its solutions face challenges such as insufficient process transparency and significant deviations from human logical reasoning.

In comparison, AutoKaggle adopt hierarchical systems (Hong et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024b; Chi et al., 2024) to complete tasks ... separately design two agents for the code planning and code generation respectively (Hong et al., 2024), and use unit tests (Zhang et al., 2024b) to verify the quality of code generation.

Evaluation metric. We evaluate the capability of the AutoKaggle from four perspectives ... The first two metrics refer to Mle-bench ... The last two metrics come from Data Interpreter (Chan et al., 2024), we made modifications to adapt them to the evaluation of our framework.

notes: Data-contamination / OOD caveat honestly reported: tasks 1-4 are classic competitions potentially in GPT-4o/O1-mini training data (valid submission 0.90, CS 0.842), tasks 5-8 are recent OOD competitions with lower 0.75 / 0.800, described as 'only marginal performance degradation.' Mixed model behavior: o1-mini Planner generated overly complex plans that increased development difficulty but gave highest average normalized score when executed. Evaluation is on only 8 tasks and uses author-adapted metrics. Paper was rejected.
